Unit Testing the Service Function

Fake timers pin down 'now', so the cutoff escalateOverdueTickets computes is something a test can assert on exactly.

escalateOverdueTickets(thresholdHours) computes its cutoff from Date.now() — the same function called twice, a millisecond apart, would compute two slightly different cutoffs, which makes "assert the exact where Prisma was called with" impossible without pinning down what "now" means for the test:

// Figure 6.12: pinning "now" with fake timers (tests/unit/ticket.service.test.js, excerpt)
beforeEach(() => {
  jest.useFakeTimers().setSystemTime(new Date('2026-01-10T12:00:00Z'));
});

afterEach(() => {
  jest.useRealTimers();
});

it('only looks for open tickets past the threshold that have not already been escalated', async () => {
  mockPrisma.ticket.findMany.mockResolvedValue([]);

  await escalateOverdueTickets(24);

  expect(mockPrisma.ticket.findMany).toHaveBeenCalledWith({
    where: { status: 'open', createdAt: { lte: new Date('2026-01-09T12:00:00Z') }, slaBreachedAt: null },
    select: { id: true },
  });
});

jest.useFakeTimers().setSystemTime(...) freezes what Date.now() and new Date() return for the duration of the test, so 24 hours before the frozen instant is a fixed, predictable value — 2026-01-09T12:00:00Z — not "whenever this test happens to run minus a day." Without it, the assertion above would need something looser (expect.any(Date), or checking the cutoff falls within a range), which checks a lot less about whether the threshold math is actually right.

The rest of the suite mocks ticket.findMany/ticket.update and spies on domainEvents.emit exactly as every other ticket.service.js test already does (Week 5's "Spying on the Shared Emitter") — confirming each returned ticket gets marked slaBreachedAt and emits ticket.sla_breached, and that zero overdue tickets means zero updates and zero emits.
